Across four benchmarks covering different input formats, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPI's detection accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points. Using the same encoder, JDPI achieves slightly higher ROC-AUC on one benchmark and stays within 0.017 of the baseline across all four. With dataset-specific adaptation, JDPI exceeds the released Llama Guard 3-8B baseline by 0.173-0.310 in ROC-AUC across the four benchmarks. In multi-turn replay on TomGibbs, JDPI uses accumulated user history as the conversation unfolds, achieving higher conversation-level accuracy than when it uses the current turn alone. Across 12 directed transfers, JDPI outperforms the classifier by an average of 1.59 percentage points in accuracy, demonstrating stronger cross-dataset robustness.

title: PGPO: Prototype-Guided Progressive Obfuscation for Privacy-Preserving LLM-Enhanced Recommendation
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026
summary: LLM-enhanced recommender systems encode item side information into semantic embeddings, but these embeddings may leak sensitive textual attributes through inversion attacks. Existing input-side defenses rely on trusted collection or local token perturbation, often disrupting the inter-item semantic topology needed for recommendation. To address it, we introduce relational fidelity as the key objective, requiring semantic shift for privacy while preserving relative item relations for utility. Based on this principle, we propose prototype-guided progressive obfuscation (PGPO), which learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words and propagates them through a static semantic graph. PGPO is optimized with GRPO using individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint rewards. Experiments on two benchmarks show strong inversion defense with near-upper-bound recommendation performance. The code is available at this https URL .

title: Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling
summary: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with trained NIST assessors, frontier LLM judges, and recently proposed per-topic classifiers. Our results show that ExecJudges agrees with NIST assessors at the level of the Claude Sonnet 5.5 LLM judges on TREC DL 2019-2021. With a small number of human labels per topic, the ExecJudges-L variant agrees with NIST more than per-topic classifiers with the same labels on all seven collections, and either exceeds the agreement of LLM judges provided the same labels or is within about 0.05 of it in Krippendorff's alpha. The labels rank the official TREC DL runs with Kendall's tau of 0.87 to 0.94, and writing the programs incurs a one-time cost of $0.17 to $0.49 per topic, with no additional costs for grading. Our results suggest that ExecJudges offers a reproducible, inspectable, efficient and cost-effective alternative to LLM judges for labeling deep result pools for system evaluation or ranking improvements.

title: RummiAlgebra: A Polynomial Representation Framework for Game-Based Algebra Learning with Jokers
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Software: this https URL
summary: Connecting symbolic expressions to manipulable objects is a recurring challenge in introductory algebra. This paper presents RummiAlgebra, a design-oriented framework and browser-based prototype that maps a Rummikub-style tile-rearrangement task to polynomial addition, common-factor extraction, finite geometric sums, and context-dependent substitution. A numbered colored tile is encoded as a monomial c x^v, while a physical joker is represented by a distinct symbol J_i whose algebraic role is fixed only for a particular candidate arrangement. We define admissible polynomial forms for runs and groups and establish an inventory-conservation invariant. A soundness-and-completeness proof shows that physical-tile accounting together with the algebraic run/group templates characterizes valid final arrangements under the stated classroom rules; polynomial equality alone is insufficient. Four detailed examples illustrate decomposition, competing factorizations, one- and two-joker substitutions, and optimization as an optional extension. A targeted review distinguishes the approach from established Rummikub solvers, Rummikub-inspired arithmetic-sequence activities, algebra-tile manipulatives, and polynomial games. The prototype implements six small challenges and a separate rule-and-expression checker; their optimal scores were checked against an independent exhaustive reference enumerator. These checks establish agreement for the examples but do not establish learning effectiveness or novelty of the underlying algebraic operations. We close with a classroom sequence, assessment constructs, and a controlled evaluation protocol. The claimed contribution is a formally specified pedagogical correspondence and an interactive proof-oriented activity, not a new asymptotically faster Rummikub solver.

title: Decent Work Standards and Non-Conventional Work: Measurement Gaps and Uneven Capability Formation in Kenya's Online Platform Labour Markets
comment: 20 pages
summary: Online freelancing through digital platforms is a precarious but sought-after livelihood pathway in contexts with weaker conventional labour markets. This article examines how worker-level decent-work assessments intersect with livelihood strategies and outcomes among experienced online freelancers in Kenya. A convergent mixed-methods study combines survey indicators from 52 workers with interviews with 20 participants. Findings show relatively favourable assessments of work-life balance, inclusion, safety and skill development, alongside weak income consistency, protection and voice. Interviews reveal that measured conditions differ in durability, whether they are institutionally provided or produced through workers' unpaid effort, and their convertibility into livelihood security and agency. The article argues that decent work provides a necessary normative baseline, but cross-sectional worker-level operationalisations alone cannot reveal the durability, production or livelihood consequences of measured conditions. A capability-informed livelihood perspective complements decent-work assessment by explaining who can convert platform participation into security, agency and future opportunity.

title: AI Surge Accelerates the Transition to Liquid Cooling: Rethinking Energy and Water Use in Data Center Cooling
summary: The power density of AI workloads is rapidly driving shifts to liquid cooling. This study rethinks and assesses the global impact on energy and water demand of this cooling transformation. Results suggest that liquid cooling can reduce cooling energy use by 25-56% relative to air cooling, offering substantial energy savings for GW-scale AI data centers. Best-practice PUE values could be as low as 1.07-1.08 for today's systems and 1.03-1.04 for emerging designs, and WUE values range from 0.38 to 2.63 L/kWh, depending on temperature conditions. We identify global free-cooling rack inlet temperature thresholds of 33 $^\circ$C for evaporative systems and 49 $^\circ$C for dry systems, demonstrating the practicality of 100% free cooling in many locations. The model finds that minimum PUEs do not necessarily coincide with minimum total energy use, because warmer coolant raises server power. Results quantify the large sustainability potential of liquid cooling and provide actionable targets for data center design and policies.

title: Human-LLM Cognitive Extension: A Framework for Studying Coupled Cognition
comment: 24 pages, two supplementary tables
summary: Recent research on the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) reports divergent cognitive outcomes, including improved assisted performance, limited transfer, and compromised unaided learning. Here, we argue that part of this seeming inconsistency arises because studies often assess different cognitive systems without making the unit of analysis explicit. Building on work in extended and distributed cognition, we propose the Human-LLM Cognitive Extension (HLCE) as a methodological framework for matching experimental designs, measures, and causal inferences to four distinct systems: the human acting independently, the artificial agent, the joined human-LLM configuration, and the human after division. The framework also treats the coupling architecture as part of the experimental object. HLCE separates performance augmentation, system-level complementarity, post-interaction human change, and stronger claims of constitutive cognitive integration. This separation can improve the interpretation of existing evidence and guide the design of human-LLM interactions without assuming in advance that these configurations constitute extended minds. We illustrate the application of HLCE with a synthetic diagnostic experiment comparing two connecting configurations that differ in how supporting information is communicated. The example highlights how distinct couplings can shape the organization of joint problem-solving, even when the final outcome remains unchanged. Overall, HLCE provides a methodological basis for designing controlled experiments and interpreting evidence across distinct forms of human-LLM cognitive interaction.

title: Hi Gemini, Who Should I Vote For? The Benefits (and Problems) of Using LLMs As Voting Advice Applications
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can provide voters information about political issues, party positions, and even advise on which party to vote for. However, no previous study explores how well off-the-shelf LLMs function as voting advice applications (VAAs). In this article, we address this gap by examining how Gemini 3 Flash advises a sample of 6,022 German survey respondents on which party to vote for, based on their policy preferences and priorities alone. In brief, we find that for most respondents, following the LLM's advice would benefit voter-party policy alignment (i.e. congruence), with a significantly stronger remedial effect among voters with low levels of political interest and formal education. However, our analysis also reveals concerning biases in the LLM's recommendations. For instance, the LLM suggested voting for the AfD at approximately 1.5 times the frequency of a standard salience-weighted proximity model. In addition, the LLM hardly ever advised voting for either Die Linke or the BSW. We conclude that while LLMs can approximate the behaviour of VAAs, users should be aware that the LLM's recommendations are still biased in ways that are extremely difficult to trace.

title: From Docket Minutes to Case Trajectories: Building Analysis-Ready Criminal Court Data
comment: This paper has been accepted at IEEE Big Data 2026
summary: Criminal court records are often fragmented, noisy, and siloed, making it challenging for both legal experts and community stakeholders to access and analyze court data to identify trends and provide public oversight. In this paper, we introduce a system for data ingestion, harmonization, and dashboard visualization designed for New Orleans criminal court proceedings data, aimed at both expert and lay audiences. Our system collects and harmonizes disparate data, generates case trajectories, and provides intuitive visualization techniques based on community feedback to analyze demographics, temporal trends, and specific case events. We demonstrate the system through an exploratory analysis of recent short-term trends and policy impacts within New Orleans, illustrating how it can support the investigation of anomalies, policy changes, and procedural irregularities. We also present feedback from a small formative study of community stakeholders who have helped co-design and use the system, suggesting that it may improve access to and interpretation of local court data.

title: CONCORD-Rec: Catalog-Conditioned Modality Utility for Semantic-ID Diffusion Recommendation
summary: Multimodal generative recommendation with discrete semantic identifiers (SIDs) requires distinguishing historical modalities that merely alter token predictions from those that genuinely reduce catalog-level ambiguity. When audiovisual, visual, or textual streams are missing, degraded, or semantically conflicting, uniform fusion and unconstrained token gates can propagate misleading content across iterative denoising steps. We propose CONCORD-Rec, a reliability-conditioned discrete diffusion recommender supervised by counterfactual catalog-partition utility. Given a fixed tokenizer and a partially masked SID state, CONCORD-Rec evaluates out-of-fold teacher coalitions over the exact feasible catalog support and aggregates item posteriors across the target code partition at each unresolved position. Rather than distilling raw token probabilities directly, the resulting counterfactual loss differences supervise an availability-masked tokenwise gate that allocates bounded modality residuals around a behavioral denoiser while retaining an exact behavioral fallback slot. We establish theoretical fixed-support ranking stability bounds under gate perturbations and evaluate position-level and code-conditional allocation across audiovisual and image-text recommendation benchmarks under controlled missingness, signal degradation, and semantic conflict. Across 20 source-compatible protocol-dataset rows, CONCORD-Rec improves NDCG by 4%; under matched 30% conflict it improves NDCG by 14.63%. The full-vs-uniform-T=16 sweep improves quality by 2.00-3.58% while reducing p95 latency by up to 86.89%.

title: MARS Technical Report
comment: 46 pages, 5 figures
summary: Modern industrial recommender systems use multi-stage cascades--retrieval, pre-ranking, ranking, and re-ranking--to narrow millions of candidates to a personalized list. While each stage deploys sophisticated models, pipeline-level decisions on channel activation, quotas, model selection, and score fusion remain engineer-tuned and user-agnostic within each scenario. This report presents MARS (Multi-stage Agentic Recommendation System), extending personalization from individual-stage predictions to full pipeline orchestration. A near-line agent built on fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B generates per-user configurations--a seven-dimensional action covering pipeline mode, retrieval quotas, model selection, fusion weights, and reranker settings--from a constrained action space. Configurations are validated, cached, and consumed asynchronously; the cascade never waits for LLM inference. Schema checks, fallbacks, and a kill switch ensure serving safety. The policy is trained in three stages: Confidence-aware SFT distills schema-valid generation from a teacher model; Format-Anchored Preference Optimization (FAPO) learns action preferences via ActionMask with posterior weighting; Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) refines the policy through Sandbox replay with a frozen reward model, without exposing exploratory actions to live traffic. Two-week A/B tests across five Taobao scenarios with over ten million daily users show positive gains on all key metrics. The largest reach +5.22% V2P and +7.34% GMV, with positive CTR lifts on both click surfaces. About 20% of requests use a lightweight Minimal mode, and deployment shows 12 ms lower mean serving latency versus production.

title: X-split Argus: Learning Reusable History Tokens for Efficient CTR Prediction
comment: Alexander Ploshkin, Nikita Stepanov and Alexey Pismenny contributed equally to this work
summary: Accurate click-through rate (CTR) prediction depends on user representations that capture both persistent preferences and recent intent, yet processing extensive behavioral histories for every ranking request is costly under production compute and latency constraints. We present X-split ARGUS, a framework for ad ranking whose history compressor and online ranker are trained end to end. The compressor encodes past interactions into a compact set of tokens that are computed offline and reused across candidates, while the online ranker scores ads through cross-attention to these tokens and representations of recent events. Training combines an autoregressive loss for click feedback with distillation of candidate-specific click logits from a larger teacher that scores each candidate using the uncompressed history. The number of compressed history tokens and the length of recent history can be adjusted to fit serving compute and latency budgets. Offline evaluation shows a 0.81% relative reduction in normalized entropy (NE) compared with the production baseline. Deployment in a large-scale real-time bidding system increases online inference cost by 15% relative to the production baseline. An online A/B test against this baseline yields relative gains of 4.65% in a business metric reflecting the monetary value of conversions generated for advertisers and 2.96% in clicks.

title: Size-Independent Survival Bounds for Routing Without a Map
comment: 38 pages, 11 figures. Follow-up to arXiv:2609.00893
summary: A walker, such as a packet carrying a secret share, must reach a known target in an unknown graph while avoiding a fixed set of fatal vertices (compromised relays in the packet interpretation). It learns a vertex's neighbours only on reaching that vertex safely, remembers its observations, and is promised a safe route. We prove that a randomised depth-first strategy guarantees a success probability depending only on the maximum degree and the number of fatal vertices, not on the size of the graph. Planarity is not required for this guarantee, and planar examples attain the bound at every sufficiently large graph size. At those sizes, when the degree cap is at least three, the guarantee is optimal among strict depth-first strategies. Whether strategies allowed to switch between unfinished branches can guarantee a larger worst-case survival probability remains open. For unknown trees and for graphs of maximum degree two, we determine the exact best worst-case success probability over all routing strategies. Explicit examples compare our strategy with random-priority frontier routing and ordinary random walks, showing how exploration order can prevent survival probability from declining as the graph grows.

title: Optimal universal sets for submodular functions
comment: Results obtained with the assistance of GPT-6 Astra
summary: We resolve the question of deterministic non-adaptive algorithms for nonnegative submodular maximization: We prove that for every $n \geq 2$ and $\epsilon \in (0,\frac{1}{4})$, there is a polynomial-size family ${F}_{n,\epsilon}$, $|{F}_{n,\epsilon}| = n^{O(1/\epsilon^2 \log (1/\epsilon))}$, such that for every nonnegative submodular function $f:2^{[n]} \to {\bf R}$, $\max_{S \in {F}_{n,\epsilon}} f(S) \geq (1/4 - \epsilon) \max_{S \subseteq [n]} f(S)$. It is also easy to show that a factor better than $1/4$ cannot be achieved by any fixed polynomial-size family. A related result that we prove is that there is a distribution ${D}_{n,\epsilon}$ supported on polynomially many subsets of $[n]$ such that $(1 - \epsilon) {\bf E}_{R \sim {U}_n}[f(R)] \leq {\bf E}_{R \sim {D}_{n,\epsilon}}[f(R)] \leq {\bf E}_{R \sim {U}_n}[f(R)]$, where ${U}_n$ is the uniform distribution on $2^{[n]}$, and $f$ is any nonnegative submodular function. This is interesting in light of the fact that uniform convergence does not hold for submodular functions: Sampling polynomially many sets from ${U}_n$ and taking the empirical mean does not converge to the true expectation uniformly for all submodular functions. The construction of ${F}_{n,\epsilon}$ and ${D}_{n,\epsilon}$ is based on a new semidefinite extension of submodular functions: We show that the Goemans-Williamson rounding technique for a near-orthogonal arrangement of vectors gives a value close to the uniform expectation, and this rounding can be derandomized, since near-orthogonal vectors can be constructed in logarithmic dimension.

title: Faster polynomial-space algorithms for poset problems
summary: We give a polynomial-space, deterministic, exact algorithm for counting linear extensions of partial orders over $n$ elements, with running time $O^*((2\sqrt{2})^{n}) \subseteq O(2.829^n)$. This improves upon the long-standing bound of $O^*(4^{n})$ attainable by standard divide and conquer (Savitch 1970, Gurevich and Shelah 1987). Our algorithm uses a similar balanced splitting approach as the classical algorithm, but applies it only to the elements outside a largest antichain. For the elements of the antichain itself we develop a formula based on inclusion-exclusion that accounts for the ways in which they can appear in a linear extension. The technique is also applicable to other problems on posets, which we illustrate by solving the well-studied jump number problem in a similar running time of $O^*((2\sqrt{2})^{n})$ and polynomial space. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with a running time below $4^n$ for both problems.

title: A (12/11+eps)-Approximation for Nonpreemptive Throughput Maximization
summary: We study unweighted nonpreemptive throughput maximization on an arbitrary number of identical machines: each job has a processing time and a release--deadline window, and the goal is to schedule as many jobs as possible. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, we give a randomized $(12/11+\varepsilon)$-approximation. This improves the recent $(4/3+\varepsilon)$-approximation of Alexander Armbruster, Fabrizio Grandoni, Antoine Tinguely, and Andreas Wiese and the $(17/13+\varepsilon)$-approximation of Tong and Xu. For binary-encoded integral inputs, our algorithm runs in time $n^{O_\varepsilon(1)}\operatorname{poly}(N)$, where $N$ is the input length.

title: Expand & Reduce: a Framework Bridging Branch-and-Reduce and Dynamic Programming
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures. Code and data links included in paper
summary: We introduce expand-and-reduce, a framework that augments classical reduction rules with a new type of optimality-preserving operation, called an expansion rule. While a reduction rule in practice typically makes the instance smaller, an expansion rule may enlarge the instance yet still making progress towards a solution. We present a simple expansion rule called edge expansion for the Maximum Weighted Independent Set (MWIS) problem. It encodes the joint choice of two non-adjacent vertices by adding an edge between them and creating a new vertex representing their union. We prove that the number of edge expansions needed to transform a graph into a clique equals the number of independent sets in the graph minus the number of vertices. We demonstrate that expand-and-reduce, using edge expansion and just two well-known reduction rules, has greater reduction power than a set of 22 commonly used reduction rules for MWIS. Therefore, it can significantly simplify methods that depend on reduction rules. To highlight the practical potential of the expand-and-reduce framework further, we provide an implementation and preliminary results showing that a simple implementation outperforms a far more advanced method for MWIS preprocessing. Moreover, expand-and-reduce can simulate both branching and dynamic-programming-style state construction, yielding exact and fixed-parameter algorithms with matching asymptotic running times. By that, expand-and-reduce offers a unified and conceptually clean perspective on techniques that are usually considered incompatible.

title: Approximation Algorithms for Product Query Optimization
summary: We study database query optimization for Cartesian products. This problem is equivalent to finding an optimal plan for multiplying non-negative integers. We call this problem multiplication ordering. We show that the problem has an FPTAS when the cost of a plan is the sum of all intermediate products; both in the case when the overall final product is counted and when it is not. We show that using the optimal solution to the well-known product partition problem does not always lead to an optimal plan, but we establish connections between the product partition and multiplication ordering problems. Finally, we prove that multiplication ordering is in PTIME (resp. \NP-complete) when integers are powers of a same base where the exponents are written in unary (resp. in binary).

title: Improved Bounds for Online TSP on the Half-Line
summary: In the open online traveling salesperson problem, requests appear over time at different positions of a metric space. A single agent traveling at unit speed must serve all requests, by visiting their positions, with the objective of minimizing the completion time. We propose online algorithms for this problem for the case that the metric space is the half-line. First, we present a $2$-competitive algorithm in which the server always either moves at unit speed or remains stationary, which improves on the previously best-known ratio of $2.04$. We further observe that algorithms must sometimes move slower than unit speed to achieve competitive ratios below $2$. We introduce a second algorithm that beats the barrier of $2$ by carefully modulating its speed, and prove a tight bound of $1.75$ on its competitive ratio. Finally, we slightly strengthen a known lower bound on the best-possible competitive ratio on the half-line from $1.627$ to $1.646$.

title: Even Faster Algorithms for Bounded Integer Programming
summary: We study integer programs $\min\{\mathbf{c}^{T}\mathbf{x}: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},\mathbf{l}\le\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{u},\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^n\}$ with a fixed number $d$ of equality constraints and constraint coefficients of absolute value at most $N$. Chen, Mao, and Zhang recently solved such programs in almost $N^{2d}$ time. We show that any polynomial saving for $(\min,+)$-convolution carries over to this problem. If witnessed $(\min,+)$-convolution of arrays of length $m$ can be computed in $\tilde{O}(m^{\rho})$ time with error probability $p$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ bounded integer programming can be solved in $\tilde{O}\bigl(n+N^{(\max\{\rho,3/2\}+\varepsilon)d}\bigr)$ time with the same error probability $p$, up to polynomial factors in the encoding length and the cost of one linear program. A deterministic convolution algorithm yields a deterministic integer programming algorithm. Combined with recent truly subquadratic algorithms for $(\min,+)$-convolution, this gives a deterministic algorithm running in $\tilde{O}(n+N^{1.99986\,d})$ time and a randomized algorithm running in $\tilde{O}(n+N^{1.9602\,d})$ time, up to the same factors.

title: Ordinal Hegselmann-Krause Systems
comment: A preliminary version will appear in the proceedings of WINE 2026
summary: We study opinion formation in the popular Hegselmann-Krause model when agents replace the traditional averaging update by a median update or more general ordinal aggregation methods. We analyze the convergence properties of synchronous and asynchronous dynamics. For asynchronous dynamics, we show that every HKS with a $1$-Lipschitz ordinal aggregation function converges in worst-case time $\mathcal{O}(n^4)$. For the special case of median aggregation and for the family of $k\textsf{-large}$ aggregation functions, in which agents select the $k$-th largest opinion in their neighborhood, we obtain sharper bounds of $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$. For general ordinal aggregation, some sequence of $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ updates reaches an equilibrium from every initial state. Nevertheless, other update sequences may cycle, and uniform random activation can require exponentially many updates with overwhelming probability. For synchronous dynamics, we obtain a tight characterization. Ordinal aggregation functions satisfying the $1$-Lipschitz condition are shown to guarantee convergence in linear time. This result applies to many natural examples such as minimum, maximum, median, and $k\textsf{-large}$ functions. When the Lipschitz condition is violated, there exist instances in which synchronous dynamics do not converge at all.

title: Two $(2+ε)$-Approximation Algorithms for Minimum Spanning Tree Interdiction
summary: Minimum spanning tree interdiction asks for edge deletions within a budget that maximize the weight of a remaining minimum spanning tree. We give two deterministic $(2+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithms for every fixed $\epsilon>0$, improving the previous best factor of $4$. Both algorithms respect the original budget and run in $N^{O(1/\epsilon)}$ time for $0<\epsilon\le1$, where $N$ is the binary input size. The first algorithm uses two weight thresholds to choose initial deletions that force every remaining spanning tree to contain edges at or above these thresholds. It then uses the remaining budget to further increase the MST weight through Lagrangian rounding. The second algorithm achieves the same guarantee through a different decomposition: it enumerates vertex partitions and heavy trees connecting their parts, then approximates a bounded-weight interdiction problem within the parts. An objective-preserving reduction from Maximum Components shows that, assuming the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis and $\mathsf P\ne\mathsf{NP}$, no deterministic polynomial-time $(2-\delta)$-approximation exists for any fixed $0<\delta<1$, even on simple graphs with weights in $\{0,1\}$. Thus, our approximation guarantee is conditionally tight up to an arbitrarily small additive constant. Finally, the MST guarantee yields a $(4+\epsilon)$-approximation for metric-TSP interdiction.

title: Counting $6$-Cliques in $O(n^{5.97})$ time and $O(\log n)$ space
summary: We present an algorithm that, given read-only access to the adjacency matrix of an $n$-vertex graph $G$, computes the number of $6$-cliques in $G$ using $O(n^{5.97})$ time and $O(\log n)$ space. We achieve this by exploiting a decomposition of an equality indicator function underlying, among others, the refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis by OpenAI and Anthropic, and of the $k$-Clique Conjecture by Vassilevska Williams and Zamir [arXiv, 2026]. Via known reductions, this implies an $O(1.994^n)$ time and polynomial space algorithm for Max Cut on $n$-vertex graphs.

title: Small-Space Streaming Hamming Approximation
summary: For a preprocessed pattern of length $m$ and a streaming text, we give two algorithms that estimate the Hamming distance at every alignment to relative error $\varepsilon$. They use $\varepsilon^{-8/5}m^{2/5+o(1)}$ and $\varepsilon^{-1} m^{1/2+o(1)}$ words of space, respectively, including all retained pattern information. Each estimate is reported as soon as its window ends, and all estimates are simultaneously correct with high probability. The prior space bounds are $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3/2}\sqrt{m})$, due to Chan et al. [CGK+20], and $\widetilde{O}((m/\varepsilon)^{2/3})$, a consequence of their results and those of Clifford, Kociumaka, and Porat [CKP18]. For $\varepsilon=\Theta(m^{-a})$, the better of our two bounds improves on both prior space exponents for every fixed $0<a<1/2$. A Fourier matcher uses $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}(m/K)^2)$ words to estimate each distance $d$ within $\varepsilon(d+K)$, giving relative error at most $2\varepsilon$ for $d\ge K$. A threshold matcher based on random-prime residue refinements and the multi-stream dictionary matching algorithm of Golan, Kopelowitz, and Porat [GKP18] gives our second space bound directly. Combining it with the Fourier matcher gives the first. Both space bounds extend to $L_1$ matching over polynomially bounded integer symbols.

title: SotSort: a stable quicksort with a tunable buffer
comment: 4 pages. Code, tests and raw measurements: this https URL
summary: SotSort is a stable comparison sort whose single code path runs with anything from a fixed 16 KB buffer to a full n-element buffer. Its core is a stable quicksort that partitions blocks through the buffer and gathers them with rotations. This report summarises the design, states which parts are borrowed, and compares an implementation against blitsort, fluxsort, glidesort, driftsort, GrailSort and WikiSort. On one 2-vCPU machine, with 32- and 64-bit integers, the constant-memory mode takes between 0.19 and 0.75 of blitsort's time on 16 of 22 input classes and between 0.94 and 1.09 on the other six. With a comparator that rules out the vector partition it is slower than blitsort on 7 of 11 classes, by up to 2.6 times on sorted input. All numbers are preliminary.

title: Improved Asymptotic Approximation Guarantees for Continuous-Review Lost-Sales and Dual-Sourcing Inventory Models
comment: 38 pages
summary: We study continuous-review inventory models with unit Poisson demand and deterministic lead times: single sourcing with lost sales and dual sourcing with backlogging. Xin [Operations Research. 70(1):111--128 (2022)] establishes an asymptotic approximation factor of 1.79 for each model in its proportional-growth regime. Under the same assumptions, we obtain a factor of 1.248977 for the better of base-stock and constant-order policies for lost sales and a factor of 1.599528 for the better of dual-index and tailored base-surge policies for dual sourcing. The benchmark is the optimal long-run average cost over all policies using only current and past information. For lost sales, lead time and the lost-sales penalty grow proportionally. For dual sourcing, the lead-time difference grows proportionally to the express premium, the extra unit cost of faster supply, while express lead time and backorder penalty remain fixed. For sufficiently large fixed backorder penalties, the dual-sourcing factor improves to 1.248977. The improvements follow from stronger lower bounds on the optimal cost. We retain intermediate constraints on mean inventory for lost sales and use events determined only by future demand to bound backlog costs for dual sourcing.

title: Batch-Dynamic Coreness and Applications with Logarithmic Work via Balanced Pressures
summary: We give a parallel algorithm that maintains a one-sided $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation of all core numbers under batches of edge insertions and deletions. For fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the expected amortized work is $O(\log n)$ per edge update, and each batch has deterministic polylogarithmic depth. This improves on the previously known $(4+\varepsilon)$-approximation and $O(\log^2 n)$ amortized work bounds. This approximation factor approaches the factor-two limit for polylogarithmic update and query time under the OMv conjecture. Our algorithm is based on assigning each vertex a "pressure" and splits each edge's unit load smoothly between its endpoints according to their pressures. After each batch of updates, our dynamic algorithm adjusts the pressures of vertices in parallel to restore balance between the pressures and loads. We show that by maintaining balanced pressures we can obtain good approximations of core numbers. Our construction also gives a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation of the densest-subgraph value with logarithmic expected amortized work and supports batch-dynamic maximal matching, clique counting, forest decomposition, and coloring in low-arboricity graphs with improved or matching work bounds. We give a practical implementation of our batch-dynamic coreness algorithm and find that it is able to achieve smaller empirical error than the state-of-the-art parallel batch-dynamic implementation, while running faster. On six real-world graphs, it runs $32\times$ faster than that implementation in geometric mean and $4.1\times$ faster than a state-of-the-art heuristic baseline. On three graphs with up to 1.8 billion edges, it is $9.2\times$ faster than the heuristic baseline.
